newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Low-growns anchor Sri Lanka's tea market.
newsitem.headline: Low-growns anchor Sri Lanka's tea market.

text.p: Sri Lanka's distinct low-grown teas have become the mainstay of the local market, propelled by Russia buying and good harvests, industry officials said on Wednesday.

Rising production combined with soaring prices means that low-grown teas, cultivated at sea level to 600 metres, accounted for almost half of the island's record total crop of 245 million kg (540 million lbs) last year, they added.
"With the money they've got from high prices, small tea growers have not delayed to use fertiliser," said Bryan Baptist of brokers Bartleet and Co. "Estates are also becoming quality conscious."
He told Reuters that a preference for low-grown varieties in Russia, one of the world's biggest tea markets, and better cropping had helped improve the market.
Sri Lankan tea, the island's main export commodity, is categorized by size, quality and elevation: low-, mid-, and high-grown.
It is the world's biggest tea exporter, with shipments in excess of 235 million kg in 1995 against 229 million kg in 1994.

Production of low-grown varieties, which is dominated by private owners of small estates, covers 65,893 hectares (162,823 acres), or about 30 percent of the total of 221,691 hectares planted with tea, brokers Forbes and Walkers said.
"Low-grown prices rose 14 percent last year over 1994," a Forbes official said. He said that prices of high-grown teas, traditionally the mainstay of the market, had risen by only five percent.
Prices of low-grown, leafy grades of tea soared to record highs last December thanks to heavy Russian buying for the northern hemisphere winter, their main consumption period.

"The sudden rise in prices of low-growns came after the collapse of the Soviet Union. Buyers were able to buy tea directly from Sri Lanka instead of through neighbouring Middle Eastern states," Baptist said.
"They can't find the same quality elsewhere except in Darjeeling (in northeastern India) or Burundi (in central Africa), where quantities are small," he said.

In the first eight months of this year, the average Colombo auction price for low-growns was 112.24 rupees ($2.04) per kg against 69.93 rupees in the same period in 1995. This compares with a total auction average of 100.25 rupees per kg in 1996 and 66.25 rupees in 1995.
Last week, the average auction price rose to a record 118.18 rupees per kg.

Production of low-grown tea rose to 121 million kg last year, an all-time high, from 118.1 million kg. High-grown output fell to 73.48 million kg from 76.72 million, while medium-grown rose to 50.6 million from 47.4 million, industry officials said. ($1 = 55 rupees)
